topics.title: Present Simple
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • Permanent states and facts: The sun rises in the east.
  • Regular, repeated actions (habits): I usually wake up at 7 am.
  • Schedules and timetables (transport, cinema, lessons): The train leaves at 6 pm.
  • Instructions and manuals: First, you mix the ingredients.
  • Sports commentaries, reviews: He passes the ball to Smith.
Formation
  • Affirmative: I/You/We/They + V1; He/She/It + V1 + (e)s
  • Negative: I/You/We/They + do not (don't) + V1; He/She/It + does not (doesn't) + V1
  • Question: Do + I/you/we/they + V1?; Does + he/she/it + V1?
Spelling of the -(e)s ending for the 3rd person singular
  • Most verbs: play → plays
  • Verbs ending in -s, -ss, -sh, -ch, -x, -o: watch → watches, go → goes
  • Verbs ending in consonant + y: study → studies (y → i + es)
  • Exception: have → has
Signal words (usually placed before the main verb, except to be)

always, usually, often, sometimes, seldom, never, every day/week/month, on Mondays, in the morning

Examples
  • I work in an office.
  • She doesn't like coffee.
  • Do you speak English?
  • The museum opens at 10 am.
  • Water boils at 100 degrees.
Important!

Stative verbs (like, love, hate, know, believe, etc.) are usually not used in continuous tenses, even when referring to the present moment. Present Simple is used for them.

topics.title: Present Continuous
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • An action happening right now, at the moment of speaking: Look! It is raining.
  • A temporary situation around the present moment: I'm reading a very interesting book these days.
  • A planned future arrangement (especially with verbs of motion): We are flying to Paris next week.
  • Expressing irritation or surprise (with always, constantly): He is always losing his keys!
Formation
  • Affirmative: am/is/are + V-ing
  • Negative: am/is/are + not + V-ing
  • Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + V-ing?
Spelling of the -ing ending
  • Most verbs: read → reading
  • Verbs ending in silent -e: write → writing (e is dropped)
  • Verbs ending in -ie: die → dying, lie → lying
  • One-syllable verbs ending in consonant + vowel + consonant: run → running (double the final consonant)
Signal words

now, at the moment, at present, today, this week/month, Look!, Listen!

Examples
  • The children are playing in the yard now.
  • I am not working tomorrow; I have a day off.
  • Is she sleeping at the moment?
  • Why are you always interrupting me?
Important!

Some verbs (stative verbs) are usually not used in the Continuous: see, hear, smell, taste, feel (senses); like, love, hate, prefer, want (emotions); know, believe, understand, remember (mental activity); belong, own, possess (possession).

topics.title: Present Perfect
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • Result of a past action that is important in the present: I have lost my keys. (I can't open the door now)
  • Personal experience / ever in life: She has never been to Japan.
  • An action that started in the past and continues to the present (with for, since): We have lived here for ten years.
  • A just-completed action (with just): He has just left.
  • With not... yet and already: Have you finished yet? I have already done it.
  • For today/this week (an unfinished period): I have called him three times today.
Formation
  • Affirmative: have/has + V3 (past participle)
  • Negative: have/has + not + V3
  • Question: Have/Has + subject + V3?
Signal words

just, already, yet, ever, never, for, since, lately, recently, so far, today, this week/month.

Difference between for and since
  • for + period of time: for two years, for a long time
  • since + starting point: since 2010, since Monday
Examples
  • I have bought a new car.
  • She hasn't finished her homework yet.
  • Have you ever seen a ghost?
  • They have known each other since childhood.
Important!

Present Perfect connects the past with the present. If the time of the action is finished and not connected to the present, use Past Simple.

topics.title: Present Perfect Continuous
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • Emphasis on the duration of an action that started in the past and continues to the present: I have been waiting for you for an hour.
  • An action that has just finished and its result is visible in the present: You are out of breath. Have you been running?
  • Expressing irritation or surprise about a repeated action: Who has been drinking my milk?
Formation
  • Affirmative: have/has + been + V-ing
  • Negative: have/has + not + been + V-ing
  • Question: Have/Has + subject + been + V-ing?
Signal words

for, since, how long, lately, recently, all day/week.

Examples
  • She has been studying English for three years.
  • I haven't been feeling well lately.
  • How long have you been living here?
  • The ground is wet. It has been raining.
Difference between Present Perfect and Present Perfect Continuous
  • Present Perfect focuses on the result, completion of the action: I have painted the room. (the work is finished, the result is visible)
  • Present Perfect Continuous focuses on the process, duration: I have been painting the room. (maybe still unfinished, emphasis on the process)

topics.title: Past Simple
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • A completed action in the past, the time is stated or implied: I saw him yesterday.
  • A sequence of actions in the past: He came home, had dinner and watched TV.
  • Habits or states in the past (no longer true): When I was a child, I played football every day.
Formation
  • Regular verbs: V + -ed (work → worked)
  • Irregular verbs: the second form (see the list of irregular verbs)
  • Negative: did not (didn't) + V1
  • Question: Did + subject + V1?
Spelling of the -ed ending
  • Most verbs: play → played
  • Verbs ending in silent -e: like → liked
  • Verbs ending in consonant + y: study → studied (y → i + ed)
  • One-syllable verbs ending in consonant + vowel + consonant: stop → stopped (double the consonant)
Signal words

yesterday, last week/month/year, ago, in 2010, the day before yesterday, then, when.

Examples
  • We visited Moscow last summer.
  • She didn't go to the party.
  • Did you see the film?
  • I was at home all evening.
The verb to be in Past Simple

was / were. Negative: was not (wasn't), were not (weren't). Question: Was/Were + subject?

topics.title: Past Continuous
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • An action that was in progress at a specific moment in the past: I was watching TV at 8 pm yesterday.
  • Two simultaneous long actions: While I was cooking, she was reading.
  • An action interrupted by another action (short action in Past Simple): I was walking when it started to rain.
  • Setting the scene in a narrative: The sun was shining, birds were singing.
Formation
  • Affirmative: was/were + V-ing
  • Negative: was/were + not + V-ing
  • Question: Was/Were + subject + V-ing?
Signal words

at 5 o'clock yesterday, all day yesterday, while, when.

Examples
  • They were playing football at 4 pm.
  • I wasn't sleeping when you called.
  • Were you listening to the teacher?
Important!

Stative verbs are usually not used in the Past Continuous; instead, the Past Simple is used.

topics.title: Past Perfect
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • An action that was completed before another action in the past: When I arrived, they had already left.
  • The cause of a state in the past: He was tired because he had worked all day.
  • In reported speech: She said she had seen him before.
Formation
  • Affirmative: had + V3
  • Negative: had not (hadn't) + V3
  • Question: Had + subject + V3?
Signal words

by the time, after, before, already, just, never, ever (in a past context).

Examples
  • By the time we got to the cinema, the film had started.
  • I hadn't finished my homework before the lesson began.
  • Had you ever visited London before you moved there?
Important!

Past Perfect is often used to show which action happened first in the past.

topics.title: Past Perfect Continuous
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • Emphasis on the duration of an action that was happening before another moment in the past: They had been waiting for hours before the bus arrived.
  • The cause of a state in the past (visible result): She was tired because she had been working all day.
Formation
  • Affirmative: had + been + V-ing
  • Negative: had + not + been + V-ing
  • Question: Had + subject + been + V-ing?
Signal words

for, since, how long (in a past context), before, until.

Examples
  • I had been driving for five hours when I finally stopped for a break.
  • He hadn't been feeling well for weeks before he saw a doctor.
  • Had they been living together before they got married?

topics.title: Future Simple
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • Spontaneous decisions made at the moment of speaking: I'm tired. I'll go to bed.
  • Predictions based on opinion (with think, believe, hope, be sure): I think it will rain tomorrow.
  • Promises, offers, threats: I'll help you with your homework.
  • Facts about the future (especially in official announcements): The President will visit France next week.
Formation
  • Affirmative: will + V1
  • Negative: will not (won't) + V1
  • Question: Will + subject + V1?
Signal words

tomorrow, next week/month/year, in 2025, soon, later.

The construction to be going to

Expresses a planned intention or an obvious future (based on present evidence).

  • I'm going to visit my grandma next weekend. (planned)
  • Look at those clouds! It's going to rain. (obvious)
Examples
  • Don't worry, I will help you.
  • She won't come to the party.
  • Will you marry me?

topics.title: Future Continuous
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • An action that will be in progress at a specific moment in the future: This time tomorrow I will be flying to Paris.
  • An action that will last for some time in the future: Don't call me at 8 pm; I'll be having dinner.
  • A polite question about someone's plans: Will you be using the computer later?
Formation
  • Affirmative: will be + V-ing
  • Negative: will not (won't) be + V-ing
  • Question: Will + subject + be + V-ing?
Signal words

at 5 pm tomorrow, this time next week, all day tomorrow, from 6 to 8 pm.

Examples
  • I will be working all day tomorrow.
  • They won't be sleeping when we arrive.
  • Will you be attending the meeting?

topics.title: Future Perfect
topics.content:
When is it used?

An action that will be completed by a certain moment in the future.

  • By next week, I will have finished this project.
  • She will have left by the time you arrive.
Formation
  • Affirmative: will have + V3
  • Negative: will not (won't) have + V3
  • Question: Will + subject + have + V3?
Signal words

by + time (by Monday, by 5 o'clock, by the end of the year), by the time, before.

Examples
  • I will have read 50 books by the end of the year.
  • They won't have arrived before midnight.
  • Will you have finished your homework by dinner?
keywords: completed by a point in time

topics.title: Future Perfect Continuous
topics.content:
When is it used?

Emphasis on the duration of an action that will continue up to a certain moment in the future.

  • By December, I will have been working here for 5 years.
  • He will have been studying for three hours by the time we come.
Formation
  • Affirmative: will have been + V-ing
  • Negative: will not (won't) have been + V-ing
  • Question: Will + subject + have been + V-ing?
Signal words

for + period, by + moment.

Examples
  • I will have been waiting for two hours when her flight arrives.
  • She won't have been living there long before she moves again.
keywords: duration up to a future moment

topics.title: Modal verbs: can, could, may, might
topics.content:
General properties of modal verbs
  • They do not change for person (no -s in the 3rd person singular).
  • They are followed by the infinitive without to (except ought to, have to).
  • Questions and negatives are formed without auxiliary verbs (Can you...? He cannot).
Can
  • Ability, skill: I can swim.
  • Possibility (general): It can be cold in winter.
  • Permission (informal): Can I use your phone?
Could
  • Past ability: I could run fast when I was young.
  • Polite request: Could you open the window, please?
  • Possibility (less certain than may): It could rain later.
May
  • Permission (more formal than can): May I come in?
  • Possibility (about 50% probability): He may be at home.
Might
  • Possibility (even less certain): She might come, but I doubt it.
  • Polite suggestion (rare): Might I suggest something?
Negatives

cannot (can't), could not (couldn't), may not, might not (rarely mightn't).

Examples
  • Can you speak French?
  • I could hear someone calling.
  • May I leave early today?
  • It might snow tonight.

topics.title: Modal verbs: must, have to, should, ought to
topics.content:
Must
  • Necessity, obligation (from the speaker): I must finish this report today.
  • Strong advice (almost an order): You must see that film – it's amazing!
  • Logical conclusion (certainty): He must be at work now – his car is here.
Have to
  • Compulsion, obligation due to circumstances: I have to wear a uniform at work.
  • No choice: We have to leave now or we'll miss the bus.
Should / Ought to
  • Advice, recommendation: You should see a doctor. / You ought to apologize.
  • Expectation that something will happen: The train should arrive soon.
Negatives
  • mustn't – prohibition: You mustn't smoke here.
  • don't have to – lack of necessity: You don't have to come early.
  • shouldn't – not recommended: You shouldn't eat so much sugar.
Examples
  • I must call my mother.
  • She has to work on Saturdays.
  • You should try this cake.
  • They ought to be more careful.

topics.title: Modal verbs: will, would, shall
topics.content:
Will
  • Future tense: I will call you later.
  • Volition, promise, threat: I will help you. I will not give up.
  • Habitual actions in the present: He will sit for hours reading.
Would
  • Polite request or offer: Would you like some tea? Would you mind opening the window?
  • Habitual actions in the past: When we were kids, we would often go fishing.
  • In conditional sentences: If I had money, I would buy a car.
  • Reported speech (future in the past): He said he would come.
Shall
  • Offer of help (in questions with I/we): Shall I open the window? (= Do you want me to open it?)
  • Suggestion to do something together: Shall we go?
  • Formal obligation (in documents, contracts): The tenant shall pay rent on time.
Examples
  • Will you marry me?
  • Would you mind if I sat here?
  • Shall we dance?

topics.title: Modal verbs with perfect infinitive
topics.content:
Structure

modal verb + have + V3

Meanings
  • Could have done – could have done but didn't (unrealised possibility in the past): You could have told me earlier.
  • May / might have done – perhaps did (uncertainty about the past): He may have missed the train. She might have forgotten.
  • Must have done – must have done (logical conclusion): The lights are off; they must have left.
  • Should have done – ought to have done (but didn't) – criticism or regret: You should have studied harder.
  • Would have done – would have done (in third conditional): If I had known, I would have come.
Examples
  • She could have been a great singer, but she gave up.
  • I should have called you yesterday.
  • He must have forgotten about the meeting.

topics.title: Conditionals
topics.content:
Zero conditional – real facts

If + Present Simple, Present Simple. Used for universal truths, laws of nature.

If you heat ice, it melts.

First conditional – real condition (likely future)

If + Present Simple, will + V1. Expresses a real possibility in the future.

If it rains, I'll stay at home.

Second conditional – unreal condition (unlikely or imaginary present/future)

If + Past Simple, would + V1. Used for hypothetical situations, dreams.

If I had a million dollars, I would travel the world.

Important: In second conditional, we use were for all persons (If I were you...).

Third conditional – unreal past (regret about the past)

If + Past Perfect, would have + V3. Refers to situations that cannot be changed.

If I had known, I would have told you.

Mixed conditionals

Combination of second and third types: condition in the past – result in the present, or vice versa.

  • If I had studied medicine (in the past), I would be a doctor now (now).
  • If I were rich (now), I would have bought that house (in the past).

topics.title: Conditionals with unless, provided, as long as
topics.content:
Unless

Used instead of if not. After unless, the verb is always in the affirmative.

Unless you hurry, you'll be late. (= If you don't hurry...)

Provided / providing (that)

On condition that.

You can go out provided you finish your homework.

As long as

On condition that; provided that.

You can stay as long as you are quiet.

In case

To prepare for a possible situation. Often used with should.

Take an umbrella in case it rains.

topics.title: Passive Voice
topics.content:
When is it used?
  • The doer of the action is unknown or unimportant.
  • We want to emphasise the action itself rather than who performed it.
Formation

to be (in the appropriate tense) + V3 (past participle)

Passive tense table
  • Present Simple: am/is/are + V3 – The letter is written.
  • Past Simple: was/were + V3 – The letter was written.
  • Future Simple: will be + V3 – The letter will be written.
  • Present Continuous: am/is/are being + V3 – The letter is being written.
  • Past Continuous: was/were being + V3 – The letter was being written.
  • Present Perfect: have/has been + V3 – The letter has been written.
  • Past Perfect: had been + V3 – The letter had been written.
  • Future Perfect: will have been + V3 – The letter will have been written.
Agent

Introduced by the preposition by: The book was written by Pushkin.

Examples
  • English is spoken all over the world.
  • The house was built in 1990.
  • Dinner is being cooked now.

topics.title: Infinitive vs Gerund
topics.content:
Gerund (V-ing)
  • After verbs expressing enjoyment/avoidance: enjoy, mind, finish, give up, can't stand, avoid, suggest, recommend.
  • After prepositions: interested in, good at, instead of, before, after.
  • As the subject: Swimming is good for you.
Infinitive with to
  • After verbs expressing desire/intention: want, hope, decide, plan, promise, refuse, learn.
  • After adjectives: It's easy to do, glad to see, sorry to hear.
  • To express purpose: I came to help.
Verbs that can take both (sometimes with a difference in meaning)
  • remember: remember doing (recall a past action), remember to do (not forget to do)
  • forget: forget doing (forget a past action), forget to do (fail to remember to do)
  • stop: stop doing (cease an action), stop to do (interrupt to do something else)
  • try: try doing (experiment), try to do (attempt, make an effort)
  • regret: regret doing (feel sorry about a past action), regret to say/to inform (say with regret)
  • go on: go on doing (continue the same action), go on to do (move on to the next action)
Examples
  • I enjoy reading.
  • He decided to leave.
  • I remember locking the door. (I recall that I locked it)
  • I remembered to lock the door. (I didn't forget to lock it)

topics.title: Phrasal Verbs
topics.content:
What is a phrasal verb?

A combination of a verb with a preposition or an adverb, whose meaning often differs from the original verb.

Types of phrasal verbs
  • Intransitive (no object): The plane took off.
  • Transitive separable: The object can come between the verb and the particle. He put on his coat. / He put his coat on.
  • Transitive inseparable: The object always follows the particle. I'm looking for my keys.
Most common phrasal verbs (Intermediate)
  • get up – rise from bed
  • get on / off – board / leave a vehicle
  • look after – take care of
  • look for – search for
  • look forward to – anticipate eagerly (+ gerund)
  • turn on / off – switch on/off
  • put on / take off – put on clothing / remove
  • give up – quit a habit, surrender
  • run out of – exhaust the supply of
  • take care of – look after
  • go on – continue
  • come back – return
Examples
  • I need to look after my little brother.
  • She gave up smoking.
  • We've run out of milk.

topics.title: Idioms
topics.content:
What is an idiom?

A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be deduced from the meanings of its individual words.

Examples of common idioms
  • break a leg – good luck! (in the theatre)
  • hit the sack – go to sleep
  • under the weather – feel unwell
  • once in a blue moon – very rarely
  • cost an arm and a leg – be very expensive
  • piece of cake – very easy
  • spill the beans – reveal a secret
  • be in the same boat – be in the same situation
  • call it a day – stop working for the day
  • when pigs fly – never
Examples in sentences
  • I feel a bit under the weather today.
  • He only visits us once in a blue moon.
  • The exam was a piece of cake.

topics.title: Word Formation
topics.content:
Main methods
  • Affixation (prefixes and suffixes)
  • Conversion – a word changes its part of speech without changing form (email → to email, bottle → to bottle)
  • Compounding – joining two words (notebook, bedroom, mother-in-law)
Most productive suffixes
  • -er / -or – agent (teacher, actor)
  • -tion / -sion – nouns (information, decision)
  • -ment – nouns (development, environment)
  • -ity – nouns (possibility, ability)
  • -ness – nouns (happiness, kindness)
  • -able / -ible – adjectives (comfortable, visible)
  • -ful / -less – adjectives (careful, careless)
  • -ive – adjectives (attractive, expensive)
  • -ly – adverbs (quickly, happily)
Main prefixes
  • un- / in- / im- / il- / ir- / dis- – negation (unhappy, impossible, illegal, irregular, dislike)
  • re- – again (rewrite, rebuild)
  • over- – excessively (overeat, overwork)
  • under- – insufficiently (underestimate)
  • mis- – wrongly (misunderstand)
  • pre- – before (prepay, preview)
  • post- – after (postgraduate)

topics.title: Collocations
topics.content:
What are collocations?

Fixed combinations of words that frequently appear together. Knowing collocations helps you sound natural and choose words correctly.

Examples of collocations with make and do
  • make a mistake, make a decision, make an effort, make money, make a phone call, make progress, make sure
  • do homework, do business, do a favour, do the shopping, do research, do harm, do one's best
Adjective + noun
  • heavy rain, strong wind, light breakfast, fast food, quick meal, high temperature, low price
Verb + preposition / adverb
  • depend on, belong to, listen to, wait for, pay for, succeed in, consist of, result in
Examples in sentences
  • I need to make a decision soon.
  • She did the shopping yesterday.
  • There was heavy rain last night.

topics.title: Future in the Past Tenses
topics.content:
What are they?

The future from the perspective of the past. Used in narratives and reported speech to talk about what was expected to happen after a certain point in the past.

Formation
  • Future Simple in the Past: would + V1 (I knew he would come.)
  • Future Continuous in the Past: would be + V-ing (He said he would be waiting.)
  • Future Perfect in the Past: would have + V3 (I thought they would have finished by then.)
  • was/were going to: She was going to call, but she forgot.
When are they used?
  • In reported speech after past tense verbs: He promised he would help.
  • To express an unfulfilled intention: I was going to study, but I was too tired.
Examples
  • I didn't expect that she would arrive so early.
  • They were going to travel abroad, but they changed their plans.

topics.title: Subjunctive Mood
topics.content:
What is the subjunctive mood?

It expresses unreal, desirable, or hypothetical actions.

Main uses
  • After wish: I wish I were rich. (regret about the present) / I wish I had studied harder. (regret about the past) / I wish you would stop smoking. (wish for the future, irritation)
  • In as if / as though constructions: He talks as if he were an expert. (comparison with an unreal situation)
  • After it's time / would rather: It's time you went to bed. / I'd rather you didn't tell anyone.
  • After verbs like demand, suggest, insist, recommend + that... (in British English often with should, in American English with bare infinitive): I suggest that he go to the doctor. / I insist that she be present.
Important!

In the subjunctive, we use were for all persons (not was).

Examples
  • I wish I were taller.
  • If only I had known the truth.
  • He suggested that she apply for the job.

topics.title: Inversion
topics.content:
What is inversion?

Reversing the normal word order (subject + verb). Often used for emphasis or in certain grammatical constructions.

Cases of inversion
  • In questions: Do you like coffee?
  • After negative adverbials at the beginning of a sentence: Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset. / Not only did he come, but he also brought a gift. / Hardly had I arrived when it started to rain.
  • In conditional sentences without if: Had I known, I would have come. (= If I had known...)
  • After so, such at the beginning of a sentence: So beautiful was the view that we couldn't leave. / Such was the noise that I couldn't sleep.
  • With only: Only then did I understand. / Only later did she realise her mistake.
  • After neither, nor: I don't like it. – Neither do I.
  • In exclamations: What a lovely day it is!
Examples
  • Never before had I felt so happy.
  • Were she my daughter, I would be proud.

topics.title: Essay Writing
topics.content:
Essay structure
  1. Introduction – present the topic, grab attention, state the thesis (main idea).
  2. Body paragraphs – 2-3 paragraphs, each with a separate argument supported by examples.
  3. Conclusion – summarise, restate the thesis, give a final comment.
Types of essays
  • Opinion essay – express your opinion on an issue.
  • For and against essay – present arguments for and against.
  • Cause and effect essay – describe causes and effects.
  • Problem-solution essay – discuss a problem and propose solutions.
Useful phrases
  • Introduction: Nowadays, it is widely believed that...; In this essay, I will discuss...
  • Arguments: Firstly, ...; Moreover, ...; In addition, ...; On the one hand, ...; On the other hand, ...
  • Examples: For example, ...; For instance, ...; such as...
  • Conclusion: In conclusion, ...; To sum up, ...; All things considered, ...
Style

Academic essays should be formal: avoid contractions (don't → do not), colloquial language, and overly simple sentences. Use linking words for coherence.

topics.title: Business Correspondence
topics.content:
Structure of a business letter
  1. Sender's address (top right) – without name.
  2. Date – below the address.
  3. Recipient's address (left, below the date).
  4. Salutation: Dear Mr. Smith, / Dear Ms. Johnson, / Dear Sir or Madam, (if the name is unknown).
  5. Subject line: briefly what the letter is about.
  6. Body: clear, to the point, broken into paragraphs.
  7. Closing phrase: Yours sincerely, (if you used a name) / Yours faithfully, (if you used Dear Sir/Madam).
  8. Signature and name.
Useful phrases
  • I am writing to inquire about... – to ask about...
  • I would be grateful if you could... – polite request.
  • Please find attached... – attachment.
  • I look forward to hearing from you. – expect a reply.
  • Thank you for your prompt reply. – thanks for a quick response.
Emails

Less formal but still require politeness. A subject line is mandatory. Salutation: Hi John, / Hello Anna, (if colleagues). Closing: Best regards, / Kind regards, / Thanks.

topics.title: CV and Cover Letter
topics.content:
CV / Resume
  • Personal details: name, contacts (phone, email, address).
  • Objective / Summary: briefly about goals and strengths (optional).
  • Education: university, faculty, years, degree.
  • Work experience: reverse chronological order, with duties and achievements.
  • Skills: key skills (languages, software, professional competencies).
  • Achievements / Awards: if any.
  • References: can say "available upon request".
Cover Letter
  • Heading: your contacts, date, employer's contacts.
  • Salutation: Dear Hiring Manager, / Dear Mr. Smith,
  • Introduction: which position you are applying for, where you saw the vacancy.
  • Body: why you are a good fit (briefly list key skills and experience, support with examples).
  • Closing: thank you for consideration, willingness to attend an interview.
  • Signature.
Useful phrases
  • I am writing to apply for the position of... – apply for a job.
  • I have extensive experience in... – have a lot of experience.
  • I am confident that my skills match your requirements. – skills fit.
  • Thank you for considering my application. – thank you.

topics.title: Phonetics: sounds and transcription
topics.content:
English vowels
  • Long vowels: /iː/ (see), /ɜː/ (bird), /ɑː/ (car), /ɔː/ (door), /uː/ (blue)
  • Short vowels: /ɪ/ (sit), /e/ (bed), /æ/ (cat), /ʌ/ (cup), /ɒ/ (hot), /ʊ/ (book), /ə/ (about – schwa)
  • Diphthongs: /eɪ/ (day), /aɪ/ (my), /ɔɪ/ (boy), /əʊ/ (go), /aʊ/ (now), /ɪə/ (near), /eə/ (hair), /ʊə/ (sure)
Consonants
  • Special sounds: /θ/ (think), /ð/ (this), /ŋ/ (sing), /ʃ/ (ship), /ʒ/ (measure), /tʃ/ (chair), /dʒ/ (judge), /j/ (yes), /w/ (wet)
  • Others: similar to Russian but more aspirated /p, t, k/.
IPA transcription

Used for precise recording of pronunciation. Stress mark placed before the stressed syllable (ˈ).

Reading rules
  • Letter combinations: th → /θ/ or /ð/, sh → /ʃ/, ch → /tʃ/, ph → /f/, wh → /w/ (at the beginning).
  • Silent e at the end makes the preceding vowel long (name, five).
  • Stress in multi-syllable words often falls on the first syllable for nouns and on the second for verbs (record – noun / to record – verb).
Intonation
  • Rising intonation in yes/no questions: Do you like it? ↗
  • Falling intonation in statements and wh-questions: What's your name? ↘

topics.title: Differences between British and American English
topics.content:
Lexical differences
  • flat (Br) – apartment (Am)
  • lift – elevator
  • autumn – fall
  • boot – trunk
  • bonnet – hood
  • trousers – pants
  • chips – fries
  • crisps – chips
  • lorry – truck
  • petrol – gas(oline)
  • underground – subway
Grammatical differences
  • American English often uses Past Simple instead of Present Perfect: I already saw it (Am) vs I've already seen it (Br).
  • Collective nouns (team, government) in Br can be singular or plural; in Am they are always singular.
  • After demand, suggest, Br often uses should, Am uses bare infinitive: I suggest he go (Am) vs I suggest he should go (Br).
  • Prepositions: at the weekend (Br) – on the weekend (Am); different from/to (Br) – different from/than (Am).
Spelling differences
  • colour (Br) – color (Am)
  • centre – center
  • travelled – traveled
  • programme – program
  • defence – defense
  • analyse – analyze
Pronunciation
  • American English is rhotic (r is pronounced everywhere).
  • Stress differences: address (Br: /əˈdres/, Am: /ˈædres/).
  • Vowels: bath (Br: /bɑːθ/, Am: /bæθ/).

topics.title: Stylistics: formal and informal English
topics.content:
Formal style

Used in academic papers, official documents, business correspondence.

  • Complex sentences, participle clauses.
  • Passive voice.
  • No contractions (do not, cannot).
  • Neutral, precise vocabulary (no slang).
  • Formal linking words (however, moreover, consequently).
Informal style

Used in conversation, personal letters, social media.

  • Short, simple sentences.
  • Contractions (I'm, don't).
  • Colloquial vocabulary, idioms, phrasal verbs, slang.
  • Frequent use of I, you.
Examples
  • Formal: I would be grateful if you could send me the information at your earliest convenience.
  • Informal: Could you send me the info when you get a chance?

The choice of style depends on context, relationship with the addressee, and the purpose of the message.
